title: Splitting of the cyclic permutation complex after a square-order lift
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, $A=\mathbf F_\ell$, $C=\mathbf Z/\ell^2\mathbf Z$ and $Q=\mathbf Z/\ell\mathbf Z$, with their additive group structures, and let $\pi:C\to Q$ be reduction. Give the finite groups the discrete topology. Let $\operatorname{Rep}_A(C)=\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathrm{disc}}(A,C)$ [def-exc-discrete-modules-category], the abelian category of $A$-vector spaces with a $C$-action by linear automorphisms and equivariant linear maps. Put $M=\operatorname{Map}(Q,A)$, with action $(c\cdot h)(q)=h(q-\pi(c))$, and write $\tau=1\in C$. Let $K$ be the cochain complex in this category with $K^0=K^1=M$, $d^0=\tau-1$, and all other terms and differentials zero. In the ordinary derived category [def-weil-abstract-derived-category] there is an isomorphism
$$K\simeq A[0]\oplus A[-1]\quad\text{in }D(\operatorname{Rep}_A(C)),$$
where $A$ has trivial $C$-action and $[r]$ is the cohomological shift, so $A[-1]$ is in degree one. No splitting in the category of complexes, and no canonical choice of this derived isomorphism, is asserted.

proof.text: All modules below belong to [def-exc-discrete-modules-category]: $C$ is finite discrete, so every stabilizer is open. It is profinite and $A$ is finite, so [lem-exc-discrete-modules-abelian-structure] applies: kernels, cokernels and finite biproducts are computed on underlying $A$-modules with their induced actions. Thus the following kernel/image calculations compute the cohomology objects in the stated representation category.

source.place: Tag 04JP, label definition-G-module-continuous, and Tag 0A2H, label section-group-cohomology; underlying-module kernels and cokernels.

proof.text: For $S=\mathbf Z/n\mathbf Z$, $n=\ell$ or $\ell^2$, write $R_S=\operatorname{Map}(S,A)$, $D_Sh(j)=h(j-1)-h(j)$, $i_S(a)=a\mathbf1_S$, and $\epsilon_S(h)=\sum_{j\in S}h(j)$. The equation $D_Sh=0$ says exactly that $h$ is constant, so $\ker D_S=\operatorname{im}i_S$ and $i_S$ is injective. Also $\epsilon_SD_S=0$, and if $\epsilon_S(h)=0$, put $v(0)=0$ and $v(j)=-\sum_{k=1}^jh(k)$ for $1\le j<n$. Then $D_Sv=h$, including at $j=0$ by the zero-sum hypothesis. Hence $\operatorname{im}D_S=\ker\epsilon_S$; $\epsilon_S$ is surjective since $\epsilon_S(\delta_0)=1$. Constants and summation are equivariant to/from the trivial representation, so these identifications have trivial $C$-action.

proof.text: Put $R=R_C$, with regular translation action, and $M=R_Q$ with the given quotient action. Define $p:R\to M$ by $p(r)(q)=\sum_{\pi(c)=q}r(c)$. Translation $c\mapsto c-b$ bijects the corresponding fibres, so $p$ is $C$-equivariant; in particular $pD_C=D_Qp$. Each fibre has $\ell$ elements, whence $pi_C=\ell i_Q=0$ in characteristic $\ell$. Partitioning $C$ by these fibres gives $\epsilon_Qp=\epsilon_C$.

source.place: Expose XVI, proof of Proposition 3.4.5, printed pp.247--248: root tower and permutation module after Lemma 3.4.9; agent-written finite-level refinement by an explicit quasi-isomorphism roof.

proof.text: Construct a complex $Z$ supported in degrees $-1,0,1$ with terms $A$, $A\oplus R$, $R$ and differentials $a\mapsto(0,i_C(a))$ and $(a,r)\mapsto D_Cr$. Their composite is zero. Let $T$ have $A$ in degrees $0,1$, zero differential, and trivial actions, so $T=A[0]\oplus A[-1]$. Define $\alpha:Z\to T$ by $\alpha^0(a,r)=a$, $\alpha^1(r)=\epsilon_C(r)$, and $\alpha^{-1}=0$. Its chain equations are $\alpha^0(0,i_C(a))=0$ and $\epsilon_CD_C=0$. Define $\beta:Z\to K$ by $\beta^0(a,r)=i_Q(a)+p(r)$, $\beta^1=p$, and $\beta^{-1}=0$. Its chain equations are $pi_C=0$ and $D_Q(i_Q(a)+p(r))=pD_Cr$. Every component is equivariant, so these are morphisms of complexes in the required category.

source.place: Expose XVI, proof of Proposition 3.4.5, printed pp.247--248: root tower and permutation module after Lemma 3.4.9; agent-written finite-level refinement by an explicit quasi-isomorphism roof.

proof.text: The explicit kernels and images of Step 2 give $H^{-1}(Z)=0$, $H^0(Z)=(A\oplus i_C(A))/(0\oplus i_C(A))\simeq A$, and $H^1(Z)=R/D_CR\xrightarrow{\epsilon_C}A$. All other cohomology vanishes. On $K$, $H^0(K)=i_Q(A)\simeq A$ and $H^1(K)=M/D_QM\xrightarrow{\epsilon_Q}A$. On degree zero, both $H^0(\alpha)$ and $H^0(\beta)$ are the identity on $A$: the second summand contributes $pi_C=0$. On degree one they are the identity via summation, since $\epsilon_Qp=\epsilon_C$. Thus both maps are quasi-isomorphisms by [def-weil-abstract-derived-category].

source.place: Expose XVI, proof of Proposition 3.4.5, printed pp.247--248: root tower and permutation module after Lemma 3.4.9; agent-written finite-level refinement by an explicit quasi-isomorphism roof.

proof.text: By the localization definition in [def-weil-abstract-derived-category], both quasi-isomorphisms become invertible. Consequently $Q(\alpha)\circ Q(\beta)^{-1}:K\xrightarrow{\sim}T=A[0]\oplus A[-1]$ is the asserted isomorphism. The degree-zero and degree-one description of $T$ uses the cohomological shift convention of that definition. This construction proves the existence of a derived isomorphism.
